concepts.name: Objectives of RBI Forex Intervention
key_dimensions: Primary goal: maintaining orderly market conditions vs. targeting a specific exchange rate level (RBI's stated position)
Distinction between 'leaning against the wind' vs. 'pegging' — UPSC trap on whether RBI targets a fixed rate
Dual mandate tension: rupee stability vs. export competitiveness
IMF's definition of 'excessive volatility' and how RBI aligns its language with it

concepts.name: Types of Forex Intervention: Direct vs. Indirect
key_dimensions: Direct intervention: RBI buying/selling USD in spot market through authorized dealers
Indirect intervention: signaling via Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), repo rates, and moral suasion
Verbal/jawboning intervention — RBI Governor statements as a non-market tool
UPSC trap: distinguishing sterilized vs. non-sterilized as a sub-category of direct intervention

concepts.name: Sterilized vs. Non-Sterilized Intervention
key_dimensions: Sterilized: RBI offsets forex purchase with Open Market Operations (OMO) to neutralize domestic liquidity impact
Non-sterilized: forex purchase directly expands money supply — inflationary risk
Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS) as India's primary sterilization instrument — distinct from regular OMOs
UPSC trap: MSS bonds are issued by Government of India but operated by RBI — ownership and cost distinction

concepts.name: Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS): Mechanics and Limits
key_dimensions: MSS ceiling is set by MoF-RBI agreement annually — not unlimited
Interest cost on MSS bonds borne by Government, not RBI — fiscal implication
MSS vs. OMO: MSS absorbs excess liquidity from capital inflows; OMO manages general liquidity
UPSC trap: MSS securities are included in government's borrowing calendar but proceeds are held in a separate non-operational account

concepts.name: Spot, Forward, and Swap Market Interventions
key_dimensions: Spot market: immediate settlement (T+2) — most visible form of intervention
Forward market: RBI buys/sells USD forward to influence forward premium and manage future volatility
Forex swap (buy-sell swap): RBI injects rupee liquidity while acquiring forex — dual purpose tool
UPSC trap: forward intervention does not immediately change forex reserves but creates 'forward liabilities' — BOP reporting difference

concepts.name: Forex Reserves: Composition and Management
key_dimensions: Components: Foreign Currency Assets (FCA), Gold, SDRs, Reserve Tranche Position in IMF
FCA is the largest component and is denominated in USD but held in multiple currencies — valuation effect
UPSC trap: changes in forex reserves ≠ only RBI intervention; valuation changes, interest earnings, and SDR allocations also affect reserves
Adequacy metrics: import cover (3 months norm), Guidotti-Greenspan rule (reserves ≥ short-term external debt)

concepts.name: RBI's Legal Authority for Forex Intervention
key_dimensions: Section 40 of RBI Act, 1934: RBI as custodian of forex reserves
FEMA, 1999: framework governing current and capital account transactions — RBI's regulatory jurisdiction
UPSC trap: FEMA governs forex transactions broadly; RBI Act specifically empowers RBI to buy/sell foreign exchange
Role of Authorised Dealer (AD) banks as intermediaries — RBI does not intervene directly in retail market

concepts.name: Exchange Rate Regime: India's Managed Float
key_dimensions: IMF classification: India under 'floating' regime — but practice is 'managed float' or 'dirty float'
UPSC trap: India does not have a fixed exchange rate, nor a purely free float — nuance of 'managed float'
Difference from currency board, crawling peg, and target zone regimes
Post-1991 shift: from fixed/pegged regime to market-determined rate with RBI oversight

concepts.name: Impossible Trinity (Trilemma) and India's Policy Choice
key_dimensions: Three goals: free capital movement, fixed exchange rate, independent monetary policy — only two achievable simultaneously
India's choice: prioritizes monetary policy independence and partial capital mobility — sacrifices full exchange rate fixity
UPSC trap: China chose fixed rate + monetary independence by restricting capital flows; India's choice differs
Forex intervention as a tool to manage the trilemma's trade-offs in the short run

concepts.name: Impact of Forex Intervention on Domestic Liquidity
key_dimensions: RBI buying USD → injects rupees → increases banking system liquidity → potential inflationary pressure
RBI selling USD → absorbs rupees → tightens liquidity → potential recessionary impact
Coordination challenge: forex intervention objectives may conflict with monetary policy stance (e.g., tightening cycle + rupee defense)
UPSC trap: RBI selling reserves to defend rupee tightens liquidity — can inadvertently support rate hike objectives

concepts.name: Currency Intervention and Inflation-Targeting Conflict
key_dimensions: Post-2016 FRBM: RBI operates Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) with 4% CPI target
Rupee depreciation → imported inflation → threatens FIT mandate
Rupee appreciation from capital inflows → requires sterilized intervention → fiscal cost through MSS
UPSC trap: RBI cannot simultaneously target both exchange rate and inflation independently — trilemma in action

concepts.name: Capital Flow Management and Forex Intervention Link
key_dimensions: Surge in FPI/FDI inflows → appreciation pressure → RBI buys dollars to prevent excessive appreciation
Sudden stop or reversal (e.g., Fed tapering) → depreciation pressure → RBI sells reserves
Taper Tantrum 2013: RBI had to raise rates + use reserves + issue FCNR(B) bonds to defend rupee
UPSC trap: FCNR(B) deposits are a liability (not reserve accretion in true sense) — a swap-based dollar mobilization tool

concepts.name: FCNR(B) Deposits and Swap Window as Crisis Intervention Tools
key_dimensions: 2013 FCNR(B) scheme: RBI offered concessional swap to banks for fresh 3-year+ FCNR(B) deposits — raised ~$34 billion
Distinction: FCNR(B) is a liability tool (borrows from diaspora) vs. using existing reserves
RBI provided forward cover to banks — created forward book liability
UPSC trap: FCNR(B) inflows appear as reserve increase but are borrowed forex — not the same as earned/accumulated reserves

concepts.name: RBI's Forward Book and Net vs. Gross Reserves
key_dimensions: Gross reserves: total forex assets held by RBI
Net reserves: gross reserves minus forward liabilities (dollars promised to sell in forward contracts)
RBI does not publicly report net forward position regularly — opacity issue raised by analysts
UPSC trap: published forex reserve figures are gross — actual firepower is net of forward commitments

concepts.name: Intervention Asymmetry: Defending Depreciation vs. Appreciation
key_dimensions: Defending against depreciation: RBI sells USD — limited by finite reserves
Defending against appreciation: RBI buys USD — theoretically unlimited (can print rupees)
UPSC trap: asymmetry means defending a weak currency is harder and more costly than capping appreciation
Export lobby prefers weak rupee; import lobby and inflation-targeting mandate prefer strong rupee — political economy angle

concepts.name: Currency Manipulation Allegation and US Treasury Watchlist
key_dimensions: US Treasury's three criteria: bilateral trade surplus >$15bn, current account surplus >2% GDP, net forex purchases >2% GDP
India has been on US 'Monitoring List' — UPSC may ask about criteria and India's status
UPSC trap: being on monitoring list ≠ being labeled a currency manipulator — different consequences
IMF Article IV consultation as the multilateral check on exchange rate manipulation

concepts.name: RBI Intervention During Specific Stress Episodes
key_dimensions: 2013 Taper Tantrum: rupee fell to 68/USD — RBI used rate hikes + MSS + FCNR(B)
2018 IL&FS crisis + oil spike: rupee touched 74/USD — RBI intervened with spot + forward sales
2022 post-Ukraine: reserves fell from $640bn to ~$524bn — large-scale intervention to defend 83/USD level
UPSC trap: in 2022, RBI's reserve fall was partly due to valuation loss (strong dollar) not just intervention — distinguishing the two

concepts.name: Transparency and Communication of Forex Intervention
key_dimensions: RBI publishes forex intervention data with a 1-month lag in its monthly bulletin
No real-time disclosure — contrast with some advanced economies (e.g., Japan discloses same-day)
IMF's Data Dissemination Standards (SDDS): India subscribes — requires regular publication of reserves template
UPSC trap: RBI's intervention transparency is lower than monetary policy transparency — deliberate to maintain effectiveness

concepts.name: Internationalisation of Rupee and Reduced Intervention Need
key_dimensions: If rupee becomes an invoicing/settlement currency, demand for USD in trade reduces → less depreciation pressure
RBI's 2023 framework for rupee trade settlement — especially with countries facing dollar shortage
UPSC trap: rupee internationalisation requires capital account convertibility — which RBI has been cautious about (impossible trinity again)
Vostro account mechanism: foreign banks' rupee accounts in India for trade settlement — RBI oversight role

concepts.name: Cost-Benefit Analysis of Large Forex Reserve Accumulation
key_dimensions: Benefits: buffer against external shocks, lower borrowing costs, confidence signal, import cover
Costs: opportunity cost (reserves earn low returns vs. domestic investment), sterilization cost via MSS, inflationary risk if unsterilized
Optimal reserve level debate: Guidotti rule, IMF composite metric vs. India's ~10-month import cover approach
UPSC trap: holding excess reserves is not costless — the 'insurance premium' argument vs. developmental deployment argument
